design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis of published placebo-controlled randomized trials of oral nicotine products (gum, inhaler, sublingual tablet, 1 mg lozenge) on withdrawal symptoms and craving. Medline and Embase, the Cochrane NRT trials database, reference lists and colleagues were searched (no dates given); quality criteria served as inclusion criteria; results were tabulated as significant or not for each symptom in the first week of abstinence (vote counting). 27 studies reported effects on at least one symptom; 12 met the criteria (8 gum, 3 inhaler, 1 sublingual tablet, no lozenge).
can_establish: Whether placebo-controlled trials published to 2000 reported significant reductions in specific withdrawal symptoms with oral nicotine products in the first week of abstinence, symptom by symptom.
cannot_establish: How large any reduction is (no effect sizes), effects after the first week, effects of patches or nasal spray (outside its scope), or whether unreported non-significant results would change the counts (blanks in Table 3 mean not tested or not reported).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Included trials (Table 2) recruited people who smoked, mostly at least 10 cigarettes a day and wanting to stop; three included volunteers not necessarily wanting to stop (Schneider et al., 1984; Fagerstrom et al., 1993; Lunell et al., 1995) and one smokers waiting to join a clinic (West et al., 1984).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Published randomized trials with a placebo control; product started within 24 hours of the start of abstinence; symptoms assessed over at least 24 hours in the usual environment; a sample stated to be abstinent or nearly so; biochemical verification. All included trials excluded people with psychiatric or acute physical illness or on psychotropic medicines, and mostly included moderate to heavy smoking (p. 116).
sample.demographics: Not reported (Table 2 gives no age or sex).
sample.attrition: Per trial in Table 2, from 1 to 140 people dropped (for example 44 in Gross & Stitzer, 1989, with 40 analysed; 140 in Schneider et al., 1996, with 83 analysed); more dropouts on placebo in three trials (Gross & Stitzer, 1989; Hughes et al., 1991; Schneider et al., 1996).
sample.selection_effects: Published trials only. Lapsers were kept in the analyses in 5 of the 12 trials (Table 2), although the text says most trials included partially abstinent people (reporting issue 1).

exposure.measurement: Assigned product, nicotine against placebo; product use recorded in most trials (Table 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (Table 2): 2 mg gum in the gum trials (Hughes et al., 1990, also tested 0.5 and 4 mg; West et al., 1984, compared 2 mg with 0.5 mg), about 6 to 12 pieces a day; inhaler about 6 to 11 a day; one sublingual tablet trial. The authors note that use was typically below the recommended level, except in the tablet trial (p. 120). Oral route; first week of abstinence.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: From the quit day; biochemical verification required, but lapsers were kept in five trials.

comparison.controls: Placebo gum, inhaler or tablet; in West et al. (1984) 0.5 mg gum served as the comparator for 2 mg gum (Table 2).
comparison.matching: Randomized; three crossover or within-person trials (Fagerstrom et al., 1993; Lunell et al., 1995; Molander et al., 2000).

outcomes.instruments: Symptom ratings of several kinds: 4-point severity ratings (Hughes et al.), the Smoker Complaint Scale, Profile of Mood States, visual analogue scales, 5-point mood and physical symptom ratings; craving as urges, desire or missing cigarettes (Table 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: No measure preferred; the authors note that craving ratings fell after quitting in some trials, which suggests measurement problems (p. 120).
outcomes.operationalization: A trial counts as positive for a symptom if it reported a significant difference from placebo in the first week (Table 3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Placebo products; blinding integrity not assessed.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. Fractions of trials with a significant effect in the first week (Table 3): irritability 9/9, depression 1/1, anxiety 3/4, poor concentration 5/9, restlessness 2/5, sleep disturbance 1/2, hunger 2/5, total withdrawal 6/7, craving 7/11 (gum 3/7; inhaler 3/3; tablet 1/1). No differences by date, size, inclusion of lapsers, use of baselines or product use (p. 117).
analysis.selective_reporting: Blanks in Table 3 combine not tested and not reported, so trials may have measured symptoms without reporting null results.
analysis.power: Trials of 15 to 240 people; the authors say any pattern across trials would have to be very marked to show (p. 117).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 12 small placebo-controlled trials, all 9 that reported irritability found less with oral nicotine, 6 of 7 less total withdrawal and 3 of 4 less anxiety; other symptoms were mixed, and craving was lower in all inhaler and tablet trials but in fewer than half of the gum trials.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the strength of evidence for total withdrawal discomfort, irritability and anxiety is high, and the Discussion concludes that oral nicotine dosing forms all reduce the severity of withdrawal (p. 121). Gaps: (1) counts of significant results without effect sizes cannot support a high strength of evidence; (2) anxiety rests on 4 trials; (3) all forms includes the lozenge, for which no trial was found; (4) blanks may hide unreported null results; (5) industry funding is not discussed.

timeline.event: Silagy et al., Cochrane review of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking; in it only 14 of 49 gum trials found significant effects on quitting, but pooling showed a clear effect (as described, p. 120).

replication.where_it_stands: An early systematic tabulation of withdrawal outcomes in oral nicotine replacement trials, giving directions without sizes. Later Cochrane reviews concern quitting, not withdrawal symptoms; a claim about the size of the effect on withdrawal needs trials that report effects.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement is printed, and the funder's role is not described.
funding.affiliations_note: St George's Hospital Medical School, London, and University of Pittsburgh. The first author is an author of one included trial (West et al., 1984).

what_would_settle_it: A meta-analysis of all placebo-controlled oral nicotine replacement trials that measured withdrawal, including unpublished manufacturers' data, reporting standardized effects for each symptom by day over the first month.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: People abstaining from smoking, oral nicotine products, placebo, withdrawal symptoms and craving.
Each criterion (placebo control, start within 24 hours, usual environment, abstinence, biochemical verification) is justified (p. 116).

Two databases with keywords, a Cochrane trials database, reference lists and colleagues, but no search dates, published trials only without a stated reason and no grey literature (item 4 applied as written, decision p-amstar2-item4).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Table 1 lists the 15 excluded studies with reasons and their findings.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 2 gives product, design, sample characteristics, size, measures, product use and dropouts; age, sex and setting are missing.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Entry criteria only; allocation concealment and blinding were not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: No pooling (effect sizes and exact p values were not reported by the trials).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Strength of evidence is called high without weighing the inclusion of lapsers, dropouts or possible unreported results.
Variation is discussed (small samples, measurement, product use below recommended levels) and study features are examined (pp. 117, 120).
No pooling; the risk is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding by SmithKline Beecham is acknowledged, but no competing interests are declared and their management is not described.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Critical items 2, 4, 9 and 13 are not met (7 is met; 11 and 15 do not apply without pooling), so confidence is critically low. The review is transparent in listing excluded studies and tabulating every included trial, which lets readers see the vote counts, but counts of significant results from small trials, some keeping people who smoked again, with blanks that may hide null results, cannot give the size or the certainty of an effect.

key_findings.finding: Of 27 studies reporting effects of oral nicotine products on at least one withdrawal symptom, 12 met the quality criteria: 8 gum, 3 inhaler, 1 sublingual tablet and none of the 1 mg lozenge; meta-analysis was not possible and good data existed only for the first week of abstinence.

Fractions of trials finding a significant effect in the first week: irritability 9/9, depression 1/1, anxiety 3/4, poor concentration 5/9, restlessness 2/5, sleep disturbance 1/2, hunger 2/5, total withdrawal discomfort 6/7, craving 7/11; included trials had 15 to 240 participants.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, bottom row and n column (read on the rendered, rotated page)

key_findings.finding: Craving was reduced in all three inhaler trials and the tablet trial but in only 3 of 7 gum trials.
Lapsers were kept in the withdrawal analyses in 5 of the 12 trials (Hughes et al., 1984, 1989, 1990, 1991; Gross & Stitzer, 1989), and more people dropped out of the placebo group in three trials.
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table 2; the text says most studies included partially abstinent people (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: No differences in findings by date, study size, inclusion of lapsers, use of baselines or product use, with the caveat that the number of studies was small.

Product use was typically below the recommended level, except in the tablet trial; a study of gum use (Gross et al., 1995, excluded for having no placebo) found that more use did not mean less withdrawal.
Blanks in Table 3 mean that the product's effect on a symptom was not tested (sometimes because the placebo group showed no change) or not reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that in most studies people were included in the withdrawal analyses even if only partially abstinent, but Table 2 records lapsers included in 5 of 12 trials and excluded, or assumed or presumed excluded, in the other 7.
reporting_issues.consequence: The extent of contamination by smoking is smaller than the text implies, but still affects five trials, all of them gum trials.

reporting_issues.issue: Criterion 1 requires a placebo control, yet West et al. (1984), the first author's own trial, compared 2 mg with 0.5 mg gum.
reporting_issues.consequence: One included trial's comparator contained nicotine, which would bias it towards no difference; it found effects on irritability and depression.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 lists 'Schneider and Jarvik (1985), Schneider et al. (1984)' as one row, while Table 2 lists only Schneider et al. (1984).
reporting_issues.consequence: Two reports of one sample; counted once, as intended, but the source of the result is ambiguous.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion says oral nicotine dosing forms all reduce withdrawal severity, although no trial of the 1 mg lozenge was found.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusion extends to a product with no trial.

reporting_issues.issue: The search dates are not given, and Table 3 prints 'P<01' for one irritability result.
reporting_issues.consequence: The search cannot be reproduced or dated; the typographical error is minor.
